items.text: Getting a late autism diagnosis can feel like relief and grief at once. Not one, then the other. Both, simultaneously. The relief makes sense. So does the grief.
items.rationale: Names the simultaneous dual emotional experience of late diagnosis — a precise, rarely articulated validation. Short declarative rhythm mirrors the abruptness of the realisation.

items.text: 'I should feel happy — why am I crying?' Late diagnosis can do that. Relief that your life finally makes sense. Grief for the years spent masking without knowing why. Both are real.
items.rationale: Second take on the relief-grief angle, opening with a recognisable internal monologue to create immediate identification before naming the dual experience. Complements post 1's more declarative structure with a quoted-voice entry point.

items.text: Unmasking after decades isn't changing a habit. It's dismantling an entire identity — the one that held your career, relationships, and social self together for years. No wonder it destabilises.
items.rationale: Reframes 'just be yourself' advice by naming the real stakes of late-diagnosed unmasking: identity, not behaviour. 'No wonder it destabilises' validates the fear without prescribing how anyone should feel or whether they should unmask.
items.sensitivity_flag: 'No wonder it destabilises' could read to some as implying unmasking is always destabilising — true for many late-diagnosed adults, but monitor replies from those who found it straightforward or positive.

items.text: AuDHD: one nervous system needs routine to feel safe. The other needs novelty to stay regulated. Both run simultaneously. Neither wins. Neither quiets. That's not inconsistency — it's structural conflict.
items.rationale: Flagship AuDHD post: clean parallel structure, quotable phrasing, names the internal experience as structural rather than personal. 'Neither wins. Neither quiets.' mirrors the experience rhythmically and lands as recognition rather than explanation.

items.text: 'Just make a routine.' The autistic side wants to. 'Just follow your curiosity.' The ADHD side wants to. AuDHD is both instructions running at once — both failing at once.
items.rationale: Second AuDHD take using the familiar advice-that-doesn't-land structure. Shareable because it names the failure mode behind two conflicting pieces of well-meaning guidance without needing to explain AuDHD from scratch.

items.text: Masking isn't a preference. It's the brain running continuous monitoring, suppression, prediction, and performance simultaneously. Burnout is the predictable outcome of that labour — not a failure of willpower.
items.rationale: Reframes masking as cognitively costly labour rather than a style choice, and burnout as a logical consequence rather than personal weakness. Directly rebuts the 'just stop masking' assumption without being preachy.

items.text: Autistic burnout recovery usually isn't returning to where you were. It's building a life that fits your actual nervous system — a different goal, on a timeline measured in months or years, not weeks.
items.rationale: Reframes burnout recovery from 'bouncing back' to 'rebuilding differently.' The word 'usually' carries appropriate hedging without diluting the point. The months-to-years timeline is directly supported by the cited sources.

items.text: 'Persistent Drive for Autonomy' isn't a kinder name for PDA — it changes the strategy. Name the goal as autonomy, not avoidance, and support looks like real choice rather than reduced friction on the way to compliance.
items.rationale: The naming-changes-strategy argument is the sharpest insight in the PDA reframe angle. Ends on 'compliance,' which lands harder than ending on 'choice' — it names what the old framing was implicitly pointing toward.

items.text: Employers rate their neurodiversity readiness at around 70%. About a third of neurodivergent employees actually feel safe disclosing. Awareness training alone hasn't moved that gap. What would?
items.rationale: Data-grounded structural critique that ends in a genuine open question rather than a conclusion. 'What would?' earns engagement via curiosity, not outrage. Numbers are rounded from NeuroBridge 2026 ranges (70–75% employer / 32–38% employee).
items.sensitivity_flag: Figures are rounded approximations of the published ranges. Defensible as stated, but do not sharpen to specific decimals without verifying the exact published stat in the NeuroBridge report.

items.text: A lot of adult PDAers spent decades labeled 'difficult,' 'flaky,' or 'unreliable.' Avoidance wasn't laziness — it was an anxiety-driven autonomy response. And managing it quietly became a second full-time job.
items.rationale: High-recognition validation for adults who lived with PDA without a name for it. Lists actual labels they received, reframes those labels accurately, and ends on 'second full-time job' — wry, accurate, and shareable without trivialising the burden.

items.text: AuDHD routines that last: not rigid schedules (ADHD will eventually detonate them) and not pure spontaneity (the autistic side can't hold it). Flexible anchors — fixed points, variable filling.
items.rationale: Actionable framing that introduces 'flexible anchors' as a self-contained concept — no product or professional required. 'ADHD will eventually detonate them' breaks the clinical register with dry accuracy and makes the post more shareable.

items.text: Honest question for PDA parents: does low-demand parenting protect your child's nervous system now, or leave them without tools for a world that won't lower its demands? Both concerns feel real to me.
items.rationale: Names the live tension in PDA parenting communities without resolving it. 'Both concerns feel real to me' signals good faith rather than a gotcha. Refuses to pretend there's an obvious answer, which is what opens genuine rather than performative discussion.
items.sensitivity_flag: 'A world that won't lower its demands' implicitly accepts ableist framing — that the child must adapt rather than the environment. Some in the community will read this critically. Consider a follow-up reply or slight reframe if engagement skews adversarial.
